speaker: williamponall
text: Good morning. May it please the court, my name is William Pinnell, and I represent Justin Munoz, the appellant in this case. Please reserve five minutes of my time for rebuttal. Good deal. As noted in our briefs, it's our position this court should reverse Mr. Munoz's conviction for three separate reasons. It's our position that both individually and cumulatively the errors of the trial court require reversal in this case. I'm going to start by focusing on issue two of the briefs, but will answer questions on any of the issues and address the other issues if time permits. It's our position that the trial court abused its discretion in this case by failing to grant the mistrial when the state introduced a jail call which included statements from Mr. Munoz that indicated he had a criminal record and that he was seeking the assistance of an attorney as is his right under the Florida and United States Constitution. As this court has said in Walcott back in 2001, it's well-established that a defendant's prior arrest record is not admissible at trial and the improper introduction of a defendant's prior arrest is presumed to be harmful. The third DCA in the Willis case said that, quote, a motion for mistrial almost always lies upon the introduction of such evidence at trial and the error in denying the claim necessarily constitutes reversible error. And this court in Walcott cited the Willis case with approval subsequently. Here, despite the defendant's objection, the state introduced a recorded jail call where Mr. Munoz compared himself to the other individuals that had been arrested and indicated that unlike himself, they all had clean records. It's our position that that statement revealed to the jury that he had a prior arrest history and that statement should have been redacted from the audio recording in this case.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Can you address the scope of the mistrial your argument on appeal as to whether it's just criminal convictions or whether it's also references to counsel and the preservation issue that's raised in the answer brief and noted by the trial court?

speaker: williamponall
text: Sure. I believe the mistrial issue addresses both the collateral crime evidence and the defendant's efforts to get an attorney. Those issues were addressed in the initial objection to the audio after the proffer and the trial court acknowledged and addressed both of them when finally concluding that the motion for mistrial would be denied after initially reserving. So clearly the reason for the contemporaneous objection rule is to put the trial court on notice and give the trial court an opportunity to make a ruling on a particular issue and not play gotcha and raise it for the first time on appeal. Here it's clear if you look at pages 475 to 480 of the trial transcript that in determining ultimately to deny the motion for mistrial, the trial judge addressed both the request for counsel and the collateral crime reference in the auto recording. So it's our position that both of those were included in the motion for mistrial. Both of those were certainly considered by the judge when he made his ruling. So there's no preservation issue in this case.

text: Okay. The courts have uniformly said that anytime a defendant is indicating his desire for the assistance of an attorney, that's essentially the equivalent of invoking a right to remain silent or a comment on the right to remain silent.

speaker: elizabethsianoharris

speaker: williamponall
text: Well, first I would agree all the cases I cited are during an interrogation. But I think I would argue they are the same thing. And none of those cases limited to interrogation statements. The only relevance is to argue to the jury or infer to the jury that there's a consciousness of guilt because he's exercising his constitutional right to seek out counsel. So I hear what the court is saying, but I don't understand, I'm at a loss as to why this was relevant for any purpose, why it wasn't redacted, why the state wasn't on notice that they should have redacted, that they're aware of the law, just like defense counsel. And the danger is that the jury is gonna believe that because the defendant is repeatedly and I guess kind of over and over again asking the person he's talked to to help him find a lawyer that the jury may infer that he's guilty because he's so worried about having a lawyer. speaker: elizabethsianoharris
text: That seems to be markedly different than stopping an interrogation and saying, I don't wanna answer these questions until I have a chance to speak with my lawyer. speaker: williamponall
